F. Scott Fitzgerald was the literary voice of the Jazz Age, the American writer who best captured the glamour, excess, and moral emptiness of nineteen twenties wealth and privilege. His masterpiece The Great Gatsby remains the definitive portrait of the American Dream's corruption.

Born in Saint Paul, Minnesota and educated at Princeton, Fitzgerald lived much of his adult life moving between New York, the South, and Europe. This rootlessness became both his subject and his condition, shaping his obsession with belonging and exile. The Great Gatsby, published in nineteen twenty-five, depicts the failed pursuit of love and reinvention across class boundaries on Long Island's gilded estates, set against the speculative mania of the Roaring Twenties. The novel asks whether the American Dream is a beautiful lie or an achievable truth.

His debut This Side of Paradise made him famous overnight in nineteen twenty, and it codified the image of the Jazz Age youth as beautiful, educated, and morally adrift. These protagonists embodied the spiritual exhaustion beneath the era's glamour. He accompanied his wife Zelda Sayre into the European expatriate scene of the nineteen twenties, where he completed Tender Is the Night in nineteen thirty-four, a modernist epic about American decay abroad that tracks the slow dissolution of a marriage and a man. Throughout his career, Fitzgerald struggled with alcoholism, and his unfinished final novel The Last Tycoon was published after his death. It depicts Hollywood's golden age as a system of enchantment, power, and inevitable decline.

His prose style combines lyrical precision with a sense of loss. Beauty and wealth are rendered with sensory intensity even as the narrator observes their spiritual emptiness. This contradiction between form and content is the essence of Fitzgerald. He was influenced by Henry James and T.S. Eliot, and he deeply shaped modernism's aesthetic of elegance within cultural dissolution. His work synthesized American themes with European formal sophistication.

Though once dismissed as a mere chronicler of Jazz Age excess, Fitzgerald is now recognized as a major modernist whose formal innovations and moral seriousness rank him alongside his greatest contemporaries.
